Aqib Ahmad Shergojri Aged 28 vs ) Union Territory Of J&K on 4 
June, 2024 
Author: Javed Iqbal Wani Bench: Javed Iqbal Wani  S. No. 2 IN THE HIGH COURT OF JAMMU & KASHMIR AND LADAKH  AT SRINAGAR  WP(Crl) No. 220/2023 Aqib Ahmad Shergojri aged 28 ... Petitioner(s) 
S/o Late Mohammad Shaban Shergjori R/o Padgampora Tehsil Awantipora District Pulwama, Kashmir through his uncle Ghulam Mohammad Shergojri aged 50 years S/o Abdul Samad R/o Pirpora Shopian Kashmir. 
Through: Mr. Shuja ul Haq, Advocate. 
 Vs.
 1) Union Territory of J&K ... Respondent(s) 
 through Addl. Chief Secretary to Government (Home  Department) J&K Sriangar. 
 2) District Magistrate, Pulwama Kashmir. 
 3) Superintendent of Police Central Jail Kotbhalwal  Jammu. 
Through: Mr. Ilyas Nazir Laway, GA. 
CORAM: 
 HON'BLE MR JUSTICE JAVED IQBAL WANI, JUDGE  ORDER 04.06.2024 (ORAL) 
1. The petitioner in the instant petition seeks quashment of detention order No. 10/DMP/PSA/23 of 2023 dated 31.03.2023 (hereinafter for short the impugned order) passed by respondent 2 (hereinafter for short the detaining authority) under and in terms of the J&K Public Safety Act, 1978 (for short the Act of 1978) on multiple grounds. 
2. Reply to the petition has been filed by respondents. wherein the petition is being opposed fundamentally on the premise that the detention of the detenue was necessitated on account of his illegal activities prejudicial to the public order and in the process of the said detention all statutory requirements and Constitutional guarantees came to be duly fulfilled. 
Heard counsel for the parties and perused the record. 
Aqib Ahmad Shergojri Aged 28 vs ) Union Territory Of J&K on 4 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/191959536/
1 3. Counsel for the petitioner while making his submissions amongst the grounds urged in the petition pressed the ground that the activities alleged against the detenue forming basis of detention of the detenue could have been dealt with by the respondents under ordinary criminal law and recourse to preventive detention could not have been taken as a parallel measure thereto. 
Counsel for the petitioner would further contend that the grounds on the basis of which the detenue came to be detained by the detaining authority are ex-facie vague besides being irrelevant, as such,
the detenue could not have been detained thereof. 
Lastly the counsel for the petitioner would contend that against the detention order, the petitioner submitted a detailed representation notwithstanding the vagueness and irrelevancy of the grounds of detention which representation was not considered by the respondents thus, vitiating the order of detention on account of infringement of right enshrined under Article 22(5) of the Constitution.
4. On the contrary counsel for the respondents while opposing the submissions of the counsel for the petitioner would contend that the detaining authority is well within its powers to detain the detenue under the preventive detention as the preventive detention is qualitatively different from punitive detention and that the preventive detention is taken recourse to in reasonable anticipation as a prejudicial measure on account of the activities of the detenue and thus recourse taken to the preventive detention is not parallel proceedings qua the criminal activities of the detenue.
Counsel for the respondents would further contend that the grounds on which the detenue came to be detained are specific and relevant taken into consideration by the detaining authority on the basis of which the detaining authority derived its subjective satisfaction and consequently detained the detenue which subjective satisfaction cannot be put to judicial review of this court.
Counsel for the respondents would lastly submit that the representation submitted by the petitioner post his detention came to be dealt with and considered by the detaining authority and consequently rejected and that the said representation was also considered by the advisory board and rejected and that the detenue was also heard in person by the advisory board whereafter the advisory board recommended the continuation of the detention of the detenue and consequently the detention order came to be confirmed by the competent authority.
5. Insofar as the first ground of challenge pressed by counsel for the petitioner is concerned, law is no more res-integra and stands settled in case titled as "Haradhan Saha Vs. State of West Bengal"
reported in 1975 (3) SCC 198. Wherein at paragraphs 32 and 33 of the judgement following has been laid down: -
"32. The power of preventive detention is qualitatively different from punitive detention. The power of preventive detention is a precautionary power exercised in reasonable anticipation. It may or may not relate to an offence. It is not a parallel proceeding. It does not overlap with prosecution even if it relies on certain facts for which prosecution may be launched or may have been launched. An order of Aqib Ahmad Shergojri Aged 28 vs ) Union Territory Of J&K on 4 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/191959536/
2 preventive detention, may be made before or during prosecution. An order of preventive detention may be made with or without prosecution and in anticipation or after discharge or even acquittal. The pendency of prosecution is no bar to an order of preventive detention. An order of preventive detention is also not a bar to prosecution. 
33. Article 14 is inapplicable because preventive detention and prosecution are not synonymous. The purposes are different. The authorities are different. The nature of proceedings is different. In a prosecution an accused is sought to be punished for a past act. In preventive detention, the past act is merely the material for inference about the future course of probable conduct on the part of the detenu." 
From the bare perusal of the aforesaid position of law laid down by the Apex court it is manifest that a detenue can be detained notwithstanding his detention or involvement in a criminal case, as the power of preventive detention is precautionary in nature being exercised in reasonable anticipation and may or may not relate an offence and not being a parallel proceedings or else overlap with the prosecution even if it relies upon certain facts for which prosecution may be launched or may have been launched. Thus, in view of the aforesaid legal position, the aforesaid ground urged by counsel for the petitioner cannot be accepted and is accordingly rejected. 
6. Insofar as the next ground urged by counsel for the petitioner that the grounds of detention are vague non-specific and irrelevant, a reference to the grounds of detention annexed with the petition becomes imperative. 
In para 2 and 3 of the grounds of detention it is stated by the detaining authority while referring to the detenue that at a young you age having met with various separatists and other fringe elements under whose influence you developed radical ideology inimical to the interest of the Security,
Sovereignty and Integrity of the State and you have been rendering assistance including food,
shelter, finance, transportation and dissemination of classified information regarding stationing and movement of police and security of forces to the terrorists of banned terrorist Organization HM and that you retain sympathy of militants in your extreme sense by reason of which you agreed to work as an Over Ground Worker for the terrorists of banned terrorist organization HM outfit and that at their instance you have been playing a phenomenal role in carrying out subversive activities and being familiar with the topography of the area, you have been facilitating their movement through unconventional routes which prolong their sustenance as also materialize their ulterior motives at the cost of interest of state.
It has been further stated that in para 4 of the ground of detention that you being OGW of banned terrorist organization HM have become threat to the security of the State as it appears that you have been instrumental for spreading terrorism in the area and make all out efforts to secure the militants by extending them information of movement of police/security forces and that you are specialist in transporting illegal weapons and other equipments to the active terrorists in the area of Awantipora in particular and District Pulwaman in general and that you have been often found roaming in the nearby villages where reportedly concentration of OGWs and terrorist is noticed.
Aqib Ahmad Shergojri Aged 28 vs ) Union Territory Of J&K on 4 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/191959536/
3 In the grounds of detention after para 4 it is stated that you came to be apprehended on 15.03.2023 under section 107, CrPC read with 151 CrPC as it was made to believe that you may indulge in breach of peace and tranquility in the area and were produced before Executive Magistrate 1st Class Awantipora who released you after executing a bond with two sureties for maintaining peace and tranquility in the area and after you were released you did not mend your ways as per reports of discreet agencies who anticipated that you may again indulge/associate in said activities, as such,
you were again apprehend on 25.03.2023 under section 107 CrPC read with 151 CrPC and were produced before Executive Magistrate 1st Class Awantipora where you again came to be released upon execution of a bond assuring to keep peace and tranquility in the area and that you however continued to remain glued to the anti national and secessionist activities despite having taken into preventive detention for two times in terms of Section 107 read with 151 CrPC and you remain an incorrigible element and despite furnishing personal bond your conduct remained defiant and continued willingly indulging in activities prejudicial to the security of the State necessitating your detention.
A deeper and closer examination of the aforesaid grounds of detention manifestly tend to show that the detaining authority has not spelt out specifically the date, time and year of the alleged activities attributed to the petitioner after the petitioner came to be released twice upon execution of bonds before the Executive Magistrate 1st Class. The detaining authority appears to have taken into consideration the past activities of the detenue as also his detention thereof under the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure and consequent to his release has not detailed out specifically in the grounds of detention the details of the militants/terrorists of the terrorists organization with whom the detenue have had associated with and indulged in the activities prejudicial to the security of the State.
In view of the aforesaid position obtaining in the matter the detenue cannot be said to have been provided reasonable opportunity to meet the said allegations leveled against him while making a representation against his detention as the aforesaid grounds of detention post release of the detenue under the provisions of CrPC did not provide sufficient details and material to the detenue to contest the said allegations leveled against him which according to the detaining authority necessitated his detention. Non-furnishing of the said specific details to the detenue in the grounds of detention has been held to be vague vitiating the order of detention. Reliance in this regard is placed on the judgment of the Apex court passed in case titled as "Mohammed Yousuf Rather Vs.
State of Jammu and Kashmir " reported in 1979 (4) SCCC 370 wherein at para 8 and 13 it has been held as under: -
8. It is obvious therefore that the above grounds of detention are vague. 
This Court has disapproved of vagueness in the grounds of detention because that impinges on the fundamental right of the detenu under Article 22(5) of the Constitution to make a representation against the order of detention when the grounds on which the order has been made are communicated to him. The purpose of the requirement is to afford him the earliest opportunity of seeking redress against the order of detention. But as is obvious, that opportunity cannot be said to be afforded when it is established that a ground of detention is so vague that he cannot possibly Aqib Ahmad Shergojri Aged 28 vs ) Union Territory Of J&K on 4 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/191959536/
4 make an effective representation. Reference in this connection may be made to this Court's decision in State of Bombay v. Atma Ram Sridhar Vaidya (1951 SCR 167) where the guarantee of article 22(5)
has been characterised as an elementary right of a citizen in a free democratic state, and it has been held that if a ground of detention is not sufficient to enable the detained person to make a representation at the earliest opportunity, it must be held that his fundamental right in that respect has been infringed inasmuch as the material conveyed to him does not enable him to make the representation. So as the aforesaid grounds of detention are vague, the petitioner is entitled to an order of release for that reason alone. It is true that, as has been held in Naresh Chandra Ganguli's case, (supra) "vagueness" is a relative term, and varies according to the circumstances of each case,
but if the statement of facts contains any ground of detention which is such that it is not possible for the detenu to clearly understand what exactly is the allegation against him, and he is thereby prevented from making an effective representation, it does not require much argument to hold that one such vague ground is sufficient to justify the contention that his fundamental right under clause (5) of article 22 of the Constitution has been violated and the order of detention is bad for that reason alone. Reference in this connection may also be made to the decisions in Tarapada De and others v. The State of West Bengal, (1951 SCR 212) Dr. Ram Krishan Bhardwaj v. State of Delhi and other (1953 SCR 708), Shibban Lal Saxena v. State of Uttar Pradesh Rameshwar Lal Patwari v. State of Bihar, Motilal Jain v. State of Bihar and others and Pushkar Mukherjee and others v. State of West Bengal.
13. It is well settled that a ground is said to be irrelevant when it has no connection with the satisfaction of the authority making the order of detention under the appropriate law. It nevertheless appears that the aforesaid irrelevant grounds were taken into consideration for making the impugned order, and that is quite sufficient to vitiate it. Reference in this connection may be made to the decisions in Keshav Talpade v. The King Emperor, 1943 FCR 49, Tarapada De and others v. State of West Bengal (supra), Shibban Lal Saxena v. State of Uttar Pradesh and others (supra), Pushkar Mukherjee and others v. State of West Bengal (supra), Satya Brata Ghose v. Mr.
Arif Ali, District Magistrate, Sibasagar, Jorhat and others and to K. Yadava Reddy and others v. The Commissioner of Police, Andhra Pradesh, Hyderabad, and another. It has been held there that even if one of the grounds of detention is irrelevant, that is sufficient to vitate the order. The reason is that it is not possible to assess in what manner and to what extent that irrelevant ground operated on the mind of the appropriate authority and contributed to provide the satisfaction that it was necessary to detain the petitioner with a view to preventing him from acting in any manner prejudicial to the maintenance of the public order. 
On this ground thus, the impugned order cannot said to be legally sustainable. 
7. Insofar as the 3rd ground pressed by counsel for the petition qua non consideration of the representation submitted by the petitioner is concerned, perusal of the record produced by counsel for the respondents tend to show that representation of the petitioner stands received through post on 15.04.2023 by the respondents and stands considered by the detaining authority on 19.04.2023 rejecting the same. Detention record further reveals that a copy of representation submitted by the petitioner had been forwarded to the advisory board as well on 20.04.2023 which also considered the same inasmuch as heard the detenue in person on 10.05.2023 and opined that there is sufficient Aqib Ahmad Shergojri Aged 28 vs ) Union Territory Of J&K on 4 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/191959536/
5 ground for detaining the detenue. 
8. It is settled position of law laid down by the Apex court in a series of judgments including in case titled as "V. Shantha Vs. State of Telengana" reported in 2017 (14) SCC 577 that an order of preventive detention though based on the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority is nonetheless a serious matter effecting the life and liberty of the citizen under Article 14, 19, 21 and 22 of the Constitution and that power being statutory in nature its exercise has to be within the limitations of the statute and must be exercised for the purpose the power is conferred and if the power is misused or abused for collateral purposes and is based on the grounds beyond the statute taking into consideration extraneous or irrelevant material it will stand vitiated as being in colourable exercise of the power.
9. Having regard to what has been observed, considered and analyzed above, in particular that the ground of detention drawn and framed by the detaining authority are vague, irrelevant and insignificant having resulted into deprivation of the petitioner for making an effective representation against his detention, it can safely be said that the detaining authority has failed to derive the subjective satisfaction required in the matter and thus in the process infringed the Constitutional rights of the petitioner enshrined under Article 22(5) of the Constitution. Under these circumstances the impugned order cannot be said to be legally sustainable. 
10. Thus, for the aforesaid reason, the petition is allowed as a consequence whereof the impugned order No. No. 10/DMP/PSA/23 of 2023 dated 31.03.2023 is quashed and the respondents including the concerned jail authority consequently are directed to release the detenue forthwith from the preventive custody provided the detenue is not required in any other case.
11. Record produced by counsel for the respondents is returned back in the open Court.
(JAVED IQBAL WANI) JUDGE SRINAGAR 04.06.2024 Ishaq Aqib Ahmad Shergojri Aged 28 vs ) Union Territory Of J&K on 4 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/191959536/

1. The petitioner in the instant petition seeks quashment of detention order No. 10/DMP/PSA/23 of 2023 dated 31.03.2023 (hereinafter for short the impugned order) passed by respondent 2 (hereinafter for short the detaining authority) under and in terms of the J&K Public Safety Act, 1978 (for short the Act of 1978) on multiple grounds.
wherein the petition is being opposed fundamentally on the premise that the detention of the detenue was necessitated on account of his illegal activities prejudicial to the public order and in the process of the said detention all statutory requirements and Constitutional guarantees came to be duly fulfilled.
summary.ANALYSIS:
From the bare perusal of the aforesaid position of law laid down by the Apex court it is manifest that a detenue can be detained notwithstanding his detention or involvement in a criminal case, as the power of preventive detention is precautionary in nature being exercised in reasonable anticipation and may or may not relate an offence and not being a parallel proceedings or else overlap with the prosecution even if it relies upon certain facts for which prosecution may be launched or may have been launched.
The detaining authority appears to have taken into consideration the past activities of the detenue as also his detention thereof under the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure and consequent to his release has not detailed out specifically in the grounds of detention the details of the militants/terrorists of the terrorists organization with whom the detenue have had associated with and indulged in the activities prejudicial to the security of the State.
In view of the aforesaid position obtaining in the matter the detenue cannot be said to have been provided reasonable opportunity to meet the said allegations leveled against him while making a representation against his detention as the aforesaid grounds of detention post release of the detenue under the provisions of CrPC did not provide sufficient details and material to the detenue to contest the said allegations leveled against him which according to the detaining authority necessitated his detention.
Non-furnishing of the said specific details to the detenue in the grounds of detention has been held to be vague vitiating the order of detention.
Reliance in this regard is placed on the judgment of the Apex court passed in case titled as "Mohammed Yousuf Rather Vs.
State of Jammu and Kashmir
The purpose of the requirement is to afford him the earliest opportunity of seeking redress against the order of detention.
But as is obvious, that opportunity cannot be said to be afforded when it is established that a ground of detention is so vague that he cannot possibly Aqib Ahmad Shergojri Aged 28 vs ) Union Territory Of J&K on 4 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/191959536/
4 make an effective representation.

State of Bihar and others and Pushkar Mukherjee and others v. State of West Bengal.
13.
It is well settled that a ground is said to be irrelevant when it has no connection with the satisfaction of the authority making the order of detention under the appropriate law.
Reference in this connection may be made to the decisions in Keshav Talpade v. The King Emperor, 1943 FCR 49, Tarapada De and others v. State of West Bengal (supra), Shibban Lal Saxena v. State of Uttar Pradesh and others (supra), Pushkar Mukherjee and others v. State of West Bengal (supra), Satya Brata Ghose v. Mr.
Arif Ali, District Magistrate, Sibasagar, Jorhat and others and to K. Yadava Reddy and others v. The Commissioner of Police, Andhra Pradesh, Hyderabad, and another.
The reason is that it is not possible to assess in what manner and to what extent that irrelevant ground operated on the mind of the appropriate authority and contributed to provide the satisfaction that it was necessary to detain the petitioner with a view to preventing him from acting in any manner prejudicial to the maintenance of the public order.

On this ground thus, the impugned order cannot said to be legally sustainable.
8. It is settled position of law laid down by the Apex court in a series of judgments including in case titled as "V. Shantha Vs. State of Telengana" reported in 2017 (14) SCC 577 that an order of preventive detention though based on the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority is nonetheless a serious matter effecting the life and liberty of the citizen under Article 14, 19, 21 and 22 of the Constitution and that power being statutory in nature its exercise has to be within the limitations of the statute and must be exercised for the purpose the power is conferred and if the power is misused or abused for collateral purposes and is based on the grounds beyond the statute taking into consideration extraneous or irrelevant material it will stand vitiated as being in colourable exercise of the power.
9.
Having regard to what has been observed, considered and analyzed above, in particular that the ground of detention drawn and framed by the detaining authority are vague, irrelevant and insignificant having resulted into deprivation of the petitioner for making an effective representation against his detention, it can safely be said that the detaining authority has failed to derive the subjective satisfaction required in the matter and thus in the process infringed the Constitutional rights of the petitioner enshrined under Article 22(5) of the Constitution.
